name: Colin Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Colin, thanks for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the underground side for the city power company, so instead of poles it's cable in ducts under the streets, vaults and manholes, and a couple of substations. A typical day is me and my crew partner Yusuf down a vault on Canal Street splicing a medium-voltage cable joint, with a gas detector clipped on and traffic going over our heads. Splicing is fiddly, almost like surgery, and I really like that it has to be perfect.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do with your evenings?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two nights a week I'm doing a part-time course in electrical technology, and I use AI basically every day for it. I get it to quiz me on fault theory on the bus, or explain a protection diagram three different ways until it clicks. I share a flat with my friend Felix, who makes video games, and I've got over a year of expenses saved plus some money in an index fund, so I'm in a lucky spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, huh, all that and it's just a better spellchecker. Online I'd post something about how the money that went into it could've rebuilt half the grid. That's a running joke between me and Felix anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it means nothing changes, which is fine. My job is safe either way, and I'd keep using the tools for studying because they already help. Honestly the cable under Canal Street is older than my grandmother, and that's the real problem in my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Finish the course, keep saving, keep putting a bit into the index fund every month. I'd keep using AI to study, because even the boring version is useful to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, like a film that never gets going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound almost disappointed. Are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. I like new stuff. I'm the guy who got his drone licence just for fun. But disappointed is fine, it's not the same as worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still finish the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Definitely. The course was never about AI. It's about getting into protection and control work, the systems that trip the breakers when something fails. That's useful in any version of the future.

S0.say: He'd joke that it's just a better spellchecker and post that the money spent on it could have rebuilt half the grid. That's already a running joke with his flatmate.
S0.think: He thinks nothing changes for him, which is fine, since his job is safe and AI already helps him study. The real problem in his work is ageing cable, not technology.
S0.do: Finishes his part-time electrical course, keeps saving and adds to his index fund each month. Keeps using AI daily as a study tool.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, the way you feel when a film never gets going.
S0.quote: Honestly the cable under Canal Street is older than my grandmother, and that's the real problem in my work.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is an everyday AI user who is mildly disappointed by a world where it fizzles. He already has a plan, a course aimed at protection and control work, that doesn't depend on AI at all. His progressive views show up as frustration about where investment goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, as long as workers get a share of what it saves. At work I'd be the one showing people the tools, because I already use them. Online I'd argue that a utility is a public service, so any savings should go into lower bills and better pay, not dividends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one suits me. I'm young, I'm studying, I already use the stuff. If tasks shift, I'd rather be the person who helps them shift than the one it happens to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, then apply for a protection technician role, probably within a year. I'd volunteer for any pilot the company ran, like AI fault-finding on the cable network. And I'd push at the union for paid training for the whole crew, not just the keen ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where it's bad for your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if management uses it to run fewer crews on the same network. Underground work needs two people minimum for safety, and I'd watch for anyone fudging that. That's where the union matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually push the union for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid training during work hours and a rule that nobody is let go because of a new tool without being offered retraining first. That's not radical, it's just decent.

S1.say: He'd say it's good as long as workers share the savings, and he'd be the one showing colleagues the tools. Online he'd argue that a utility is a public service, so savings belong in lower bills and better pay.
S1.think: He thinks this picture suits him because he's young, studying and already uses AI. He'd rather help the shift happen than have it happen to him.
S1.do: Finishes the course and applies for a protection technician role within a year, and volunteers for any AI fault-finding pilot. Pushes the union for paid training for the whole crew.
S1.quote: If tasks shift, I'd rather be the person who helps them shift than the one it happens to.
S1.fieldNote: His enthusiasm for the tools sits easily next to his union politics; he sees no conflict between them. His safety concern is specific: the two-person rule underground. He wants retraining guaranteed for everyone, not just keen people like himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is the biggest thing to happen to working people ever, and it can't be left to five tech companies. I'd be at marches, honestly, for a public stake in the AI and robots, or a share of the profits for everyone. I'd be posting a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if robots can splice cable as well as me in two years, then my course is a waste, and so is everything else I'd think of learning. I'd be fine for money for a while. What scares me is two years of governments arguing while millions lose work at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to work with whatever robots the company brings in, train them, fix them, supervise them, because that's the last job left standing for a while. I'd join every campaign going for a share of the gains. And I'd go to the union to make sure nobody gets let go without a proper deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly for everyone else. For me, it's more a knot than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been quite calm so far. Is that still true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less calm. The speed is what gets me. I'm good at adapting, but adapting to what? There's nothing to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings and the index fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cash savings where they are, that's my safety net. If AGI is real, the companies that own it will be worth a fortune, so honestly the index fund might do better than my wages. That feels awful to say as a lefty, but I'd add to it.

S2.say: He'd say it's the biggest thing ever to happen to working people and can't be left to a handful of tech companies. He'd march and post for a public stake in AI or a share of profits for everyone.
S2.think: He thinks two years would make his course and any other retraining pointless, though his money would last a while. What scares him most is governments arguing while millions lose work at once.
S2.do: Volunteers to work alongside the company's robots, training, fixing and supervising them, and joins campaigns for a share of the gains. Keeps his cash safety net and adds to his index fund, while pressing the union for proper deals.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly on behalf of others, with a knot rather than panic for himself.
S2.quote: I'm good at adapting, but adapting to what? There's nothing to aim at.
S2.fieldNote: Two years is the first picture that unsettles him, because his usual strength, learning fast, has no target. He openly noted the discomfort of a left-leaning worker expecting his shares to beat his wages. He would move toward the robots, not away from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got five years to get it right, so let's use them. I'd want the city to keep the power company public and use it as a model for how to bring in robots fairly. I'd be in the local campaign, maybe running a meeting or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to land somewhere useful. I'd be thirty-two, with the course done and a few years in robotics or control. Not forever, but long enough to work out the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the course and move into the protection and control team. Then I'd push to join whatever group the company sets up to bring in robots for the underground work. I'd keep investing every month and stay active in the union and the campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. I'd be too occupied to dwell on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job move. Politics takes forever, and I can do both, but I'd want my own feet under me first. Then I'd have time and money to put into the campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you do first, the politics or the job move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Felix and I talk about this, actually. He thinks games will be the first to go, which is funny because he's the one who got me into AI. I'd want to help him land somewhere too.

S3.say: He'd say there are five years to get it right and they must be used, with the city keeping the power company public as a model for fair automation. He'd be active in a local campaign and might run meetings.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to land somewhere useful, with his course done and a few years in robotics or control. Not forever, but long enough to work out what comes next.
S3.do: Finishes the course and moves into the protection and control team in the first year, then aims for the company's robot rollout group. Invests monthly and stays active in the union and the campaign.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, too occupied to dwell on it.
S3.quote: Politics takes forever, and I can do both, but I'd want my own feet under me first.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him something to aim at again, so he gets practical about sequence: job first, campaign second. He sees the city-owned utility as a possible example for fair automation. His flatmate's job worries came up as a natural tangent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, if we use it. Ten years is long enough to build a system where nobody's left with nothing. I'd keep saying that, online and at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years sounds fine for me. By thirty-seven I'd have done a couple of jobs on the way, and if robots do everything by then, I'd hope we'd have built some kind of shared income. I'm genuinely more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, take the protection job and keep learning the new tools as they come out. I'd stay in the union and vote for whoever's serious about sharing the gains. The investing and saving would carry on as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested. It's a long way off and I'd have a lot to do in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too long to plan for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Too long to plan exactly, not too long to prepare. I wouldn't plan year eight. I'd just keep my skills and savings in shape and stay flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this decade go well for people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Public money for retraining, with a wage while you do it, and some share of what the robots earn. And unions being in the room when companies plan it, not told after.

S4.say: He'd call this the good version, if it's used well, because a decade is enough to build a system where nobody is left with nothing. He'd say so online and at union meetings.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is fine for him: by thirty-seven he'd have moved through a couple of jobs and hopes society would have built some shared income. He's more curious than scared.
S4.do: Finishes the course, takes the protection job and keeps learning new tools as they arrive. Stays in the union, votes for candidates serious about sharing the gains and keeps saving and investing as normal.
S4.feel: Calm and interested, with plenty to do before it arrives.
S4.quote: Too long to plan exactly, not too long to prepare.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Colin settles back into the calm he showed in the milder pictures. He avoids false precision and talks about staying flexible. His policy wish list is consistent across the interview: paid retraining, a share of robot earnings and unions in the room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for my bank account, but because I couldn't see a target to aim at, and neither could anyone else. What would help is a plan made now, by governments and unions together, for how the gains get shared, so it's not invented in a panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people would miss. I'd miss splicing. Even if a robot does it better, there's something about getting a joint perfect at the bottom of a hole in the rain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: Even if a robot does it better, there's something about getting a joint perfect at the bottom of a hole in the rain.
portrait: Colin Bauer is a 27-year-old underground cable lineworker for a city power company, splicing medium-voltage cable in vaults beneath busy streets. He shares a flat with a friend, has over a year of savings and an index fund, and uses AI daily to study for a part-time electrical technology course. He is calm or even excited in the milder pictures and plans to move into protection and control work. A two-year AGI warning makes him anxious because his strength, adapting fast, has nothing to aim at, while five or ten years let him plan job moves and campaign for a share of the gains. He sees no conflict between loving new tools and wanting unions and public ownership.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because neither he nor anyone else would have a target to aim at.
whatWouldHelp: A plan made now by governments and unions together for sharing the gains, rather than one invented in a panic.
